transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Riley Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jonas Fischer (Redwood SRE), Asha Verma (CTO, Northshore), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Priya Menon (ML Eng), Daniel Reyes (Security)
---
Summary (auto): Deep dive into token-cache handoff behavior and prefetch tuning for long-context workloads. Plan: collect KV logs, run microbenchmarks, align on warmup strategy for on-prem/VPC deployments.
Shared artifacts: bench config + dashboard (https://redwood.share/benchmarks/ff-2026-12-04) ; prefetch whitepaper (doc link in chat)
---
00:00:05 Riley Chen: Okay, hi everyone, thanks for joining. We'll run through the cache handoff and prefetch stuff, make sure we capture logs. Maya and Jonas from my side will take the deeper questions.
00:00:18 Asha Verma: Thanks. We're seeing user-facing latency spikes when we go beyond about 6k tokens, and sometimes we get a weird tail latency where a few requests blow up to multiple seconds.
00:00:30 Maya Patel: Right, that usually signals either paging from the token cache or a re-load of a large prefix into memory. Can you describe the workload pattern? Are you doing lots of prefix reuse across sessions?
00:00:45 Liam O'Connor: Yes, we have a few system prompts that are reused a lot — conversation starter templates and policy blocks. They generate hot prefixes. Also we do a lot of multi-turn, so the context gets long and the KV grows.
00:01:02 Jonas Fischer: Quick note: our telemetry shows memory pressure spikes right before those slow tails. It's consistent with spillback to disk, but the exact eviction signatures are fuzzy.
00:01:18 Maya Patel: Okay, perfect. We'll look for these signatures: sudden increase in KV cache miss rate, a burst of page-in latency, and corresponding GPU stalls. If page-in happens on critical path it will spike token latency.
00:01:35 Priya Menon: One thing: when we enabled 4-bit quantization to save memory we thought we'd get fewer spills, but latency patterns changed — sometimes worse. Could quantization be affecting cache layout?
00:01:50 Riley Chen: Good call — quantization can change the working set and chunking at kernel level. Not typically the cache's fault but it shifts memory footprints and might increase prefix sizes if attention keys are packed differently.
00:02:05 Daniel Reyes: Also, since we're evaluating an on-prem option in VPC with limited spare RAM per node, we want to understand warmup strategies so we don't saturate the local node and force network fallback.
00:02:18 Maya Patel: Right. There are two axes: proactive prefetch (warm up likely prefixes on spawn) and adaptive prefetch (based on recent hot-prefix counts). Both have tradeoffs: prefetch reduces tail latency for expected prefixes but increases steady-state memory usage and can cause eviction pressure for less-used items.
00:02:36 Asha Verma: Can you walk through what an eviction signature looks like from Redwood's perspective? We have logs but not sure what to zero in on.
00:02:50 Jonas Fischer: I'll pull up an example we captured.
00:03:02 Jonas Fischer: (screen share note) Here's sequence: high prefix reference count -> memory util climbs to 92% -> background evictor triggers -> a set of older prefixes gets removed -> shortly after miss rate jumps for a hot prefix -> the engine pages keys back in -> stalls. The interesting part is we sometimes see eviction of a prefix that should have been pinned because prefix fingerprinting changed after a tokenizer variant.
00:03:36 Liam O'Connor: Hmm, we've seen the tokenizer change during blue/green deploys and it does alter prefix hashes. Could that explain prefix mismatch and double-caching?
00:03:49 Maya Patel: Yes. Tokenizer and normalization changes are a silent source of prefix churn. If the same logical prompt tokenizes differently, you can get cold prefixes that look new to the cache. We recommend stable tokenizer pipeline across rollouts or using canonicalized prefix IDs if you can.
00:04:08 Asha Verma: We do sometimes roll the tokenizer when we update models. Not ideal.
00:04:15 Riley Chen: For on-prem, you can also add a short-lived sticky layer: a per-session warm cache that loads likely prefixes at session start. It increases startup cost but reduces runtime page-in.
00:04:28 Priya Menon: What's the best way to detect that paging is happening versus a compute stall? Our logs have GPU busy, but not clearly correlated.
00:04:40 Jonas Fischer: Look at three signals: GPU compute utilization drop + host disk I/O increase + a sudden rise in per-token latency. If all three align, it's paging. Also check KV miss spikes and page-in latency histogram.
00:04:55 Riley Chen: Maya, can you explain the 'handoff' flow? We often say "hand off" but people mean different things.
00:05:04 Maya Patel: Sure — handoff is when a request's KV context extends beyond the local GPU's in-memory KV and the runtime must pull missing KV entries from the distributed store or spill store. There are synchronous handoffs (blocking) and async ones that try to prefetch. Synchronous handoffs are simpler but cause tail latency.
00:05:25 Asha Verma: Are there recommended thresholds for when to prefetch? Like prefetch if prefix reuse > X%?
00:05:35 Maya Patel: It's workload dependent. Common heuristic: prefetch when a prefix is referenced by >N distinct sessions in last T minutes or when request admission probability of that prefix toward the top-k tokens crosses a threshold. We usually recommend conservative default: prefetch for prefixes with >300 references in last 15 minutes for heavy-production workloads, but run microbenchmarks to calibrate.
00:06:00 Liam O'Connor: That 300 number — is that absolute or relative to memory size? We have nodes with 64GB and some with 96GB.
00:06:10 Maya Patel: Relative to memory and model footprint. It's a rule-of-thumb. The bench we'll run will give you measured SLO vs memory curve.
00:06:25 Priya Menon: About prefix reuse storms — we suspect a batch job spikes reuse for a subset of prefixes every hour, causing eviction cascades. Any mitigations?
00:06:36 Maya Patel: Yes — soft-pinning: keep hot prefixes with an adaptive TTL that increases with reuse frequency, but evict less important ones earlier. Also, coordinated batch admission: when you expect a scheduled batch, either warm the cache first or route batch to dedicated capacity so it doesn't evict interactive prefixes.
00:06:58 Jonas Fischer: For Northshore specifically, you have bursty nightly analytics that looks like this batch workload. If we warm before the batch, it's effective. But warming itself pegs memory for a while. We need to balance.
00:07:12 Asha Verma: On the subject of routing — could we route analytic batches to a dedicated pool in private deployment? We want to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
00:07:20 Riley Chen: Absolutely — Redwood Dedicated or private routing policies can direct those heavy batches to reserved capacity. On-prem you can run separate VM pools or containers pinned to separate nodes. That keeps interactive concurrency steady.
00:07:35 Daniel Reyes: Security question: when prefetching happens in VPC/on-prem, what about KMS keys or HSM integration? We need to ensure prefetch doesn't leak keys or data to other tenancy.
00:07:47 Riley Chen: Prefetch is purely about token keys and attention caches — it doesn't move user data off the node. For Private deployments we provide KMS integration and you control key access. We'll send the checklist.
00:07:59 Maya Patel: Back to eviction signatures — another gotcha is prefix aliasing when you have normalization differences across clients; it looks like prefix reuse but with different IDs so cache entries don't line up. Our instrumentation includes a prefix-correlation view for that. We'll share a sample.
00:08:18 Asha Verma: That view would be useful.
00:08:22 Liam O'Connor: About benchmarks: what microbench setup do you recommend? We want deterministic runs that reproduce the miss storm.
00:08:31 Maya Patel: A minimal microbench: fixed request stream with controlled prefix creation, parameterizable session length (1k/4k/8k tokens), prefix reuse pattern (zipf vs uniform), and ability to toggle quantization and batch sizes. Run a sweep for memory budgets (XGB) and record per-token p50/p95/p99. We'll share our harness.
00:08:57 Priya Menon: Can your harness simulate tokenizer drift? That's a big source of churn for us.
00:09:05 Maya Patel: We can parameterize tokenization variant by changing normalization or using alternate token maps; that will show prefix fragmentation.
00:09:14 Jonas Fischer: One operational trick we used: store canonicalized prompt fingerprints in a separate index so if tokenizer changes you can map old to new when possible. It's an extra layer but helps migration.
00:09:28 Asha Verma: That sounds helpful.
00:09:32 Riley Chen: Let's talk about handoff latency numbers. If a prefix is missing and we have to page it in from distributed KV, what's typical extra latency? Maya?
00:09:42 Maya Patel: If you have a local SSD-backed spill store, page-in is typically 20-200ms depending on size and concurrency. If it's distributed remote, it can be 200ms-1s. Those are rough; your environment matters. That's why warmup matters for interactive SLOs.
00:09:59 Liam O'Connor: Our late tails are in the 300-700ms range, which fits the remote page-in profile. We're using NFS in a peered storage cluster for spills. Could be that.
00:10:10 Priya Menon: Are there logging knobs to highlight which path (local SSD vs remote) is being used?
00:10:18 Maya Patel: Yes — the runtime emits a "kv_path" tag per miss (local|ssd|remote) and a page_in_latency_ms histogram. If you don't have that flagged in your logs we can add it.
00:10:30 Asha Verma: We'll enable that.
00:10:33 Jonas Fischer: Another note: when we try to compact prefixes, compaction can be CPU intensive and if it runs during peak it can contend with GC and eviction, making things worse. So schedule compaction windows during low traffic.
00:10:49 Riley Chen: Good ops note.
00:10:52 Priya Menon: What about batching behavior? Our throughput spikes are good but sometimes batching increases latency because it bundles requests that trigger misses.
00:11:02 Maya Patel: Batching helps throughput but can worsen tail latency if one request in the batch needs a page-in and blocks the whole batch. Strategies: dynamic batch sizing (smaller batches when miss probability is high), early-exit for missing KV keys, or speculative prefetch on batch admission based on per-prefix probability.
00:11:23 Liam O'Connor: Speculative prefetch seems complex but promising. How do you estimate per-prefix probability quickly?
00:11:30 Maya Patel: We use a lightweight probability table maintained in-memory with exponentially decayed counts per prefix; on admission we compute aggregate probability that batch includes hot prefixes and decide to prefetch. Very approximate but effective.
00:11:45 Asha Verma: What's the overhead of maintaining that table? Memory? CPU?
00:11:50 Maya Patel: It's tunable; typical footprint is small relative to KV cache—few MBs to tens of MBs depending on cardinality. CPU cost is small if implemented as approximate counters (CMS/sketches).
00:12:05 Daniel Reyes: For VPC/on-prem, we worry about network egress if prefetch pulls from remote. Any guardrails?
00:12:11 Riley Chen: Redwood can be configured to disallow remote prefetch in private mode or to restrict it only to dedicated pools. We'll include config examples in the playbook.
00:12:22 Liam O'Connor: Could the runtime selectively coast to CPU-only execution rather than block waiting for page-in? Sometimes degraded CPU path is better than huge tail.
00:12:34 Maya Patel: Yes — graceful degradation is part of our runtime: switch to lower-precision fast path or smaller context path as last resort. But results may differ in semantics. It's a policy choice: keep latency vs fidelity.
00:12:50 Priya Menon: Any guidance on quantization interactions? We saw more prefix fragmentation after 4-bit.
00:12:58 Maya Patel: Quantization affects model memory layout and sometimes token-key sizes; it may increase the number of KV pages needed for a given prefix. Also, smaller numeric formats can change chunk sizes for attention caches. We advise testing quantization in the bench with representative context sizes.
00:13:15 Riley Chen: Let's return to concrete next steps: we'll collect KV telemetry, you'll run the microbench, and we'll reconvene. Any objections?
00:13:24 Asha Verma: Sounds good. We'll need the telemetry script.
00:13:28 Riley Chen: I'll post the script and the sample logs to the shared folder.
00:13:33 Liam O'Connor: One last question: in blue/green deploys, is there a safe migration path for tokenizers to avoid double-caching during rollout?
00:13:42 Maya Patel: Approach: roll tokenizer changes with backward compatibility layer where both tokenizers are allowed to map to canonical fingerprints for some time. Or do a coordinated cache migration phase: snapshot hot prefixes, translate fingerprints, and repopulate. Both are doable but more operationally heavy.
00:13:59 Priya Menon: That explains a lot.
00:14:04 Jonas Fischer: For the logs we'll provide a sanitized sample of the eviction timeline and page-in histograms.
00:14:11 Riley Chen: Great. We'll schedule the follow-up for next week. Thanks, everyone.
